record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: Can interactive zero-knowledge proofs or non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs be made efficient enough for federated learning, both for proving properties of client inputs to the server and for client-side verification tasks that depend on information from multiple participants?

evidence.quote: Using interactive ZKP systems and NIZKs efﬁciently in the context of FL remains a challenging open question. In such a setting, NIZKs may enable to prove to the server properties about the client’s inputs. In the setting where the veriﬁer is the client, it will be challenging to create a trustworthy statement to verify as it involves input from other clients.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the federated learning setting in which a central server coordinates the training of a shared model with many clients. Each client holds private local data and computes a local update (e.g., a gradient or model delta), which is sent to the server, which aggregates the updates to produce the next global model.

Recall that an interactive zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) system allows a prover holding a secret witness w for a statement x in a language L to convince a verifier that x ∈ L through a multi-round interactive protocol, while leaking no information about w beyond this fact. A non-interactive zero-knowledge proof (NIZK) achieves the same guarantee with a single message from prover to verifier (typically in a common reference string or random oracle model). Standard requirements are completeness, computational (or statistical) soundness, and the zero-knowledge property; efficiency is measured by prover time, verifier time, proof size, and any setup/CRS cost.

Design ZKP or NIZK protocols that are simultaneously practical for the following two federated-learning tasks, and prove the corresponding completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge properties together with concrete asymptotic and concrete efficiency bounds:

1. Server-directed proofs of input properties. For a fixed predicate P on client local inputs/updates (for example: norm bounds on a gradient, correctness of the local training procedure with respect to a published model and a committed dataset, validity of dataset format, or honest sampling from a committed local distribution), construct a NIZK such that each client can prove to the server that its submitted update u satisfies P(u) = 1 with respect to a public commitment to the client's data, while revealing nothing about the client's data or update beyond P(u) = 1. The protocol must scale to model sizes and client populations typical of federated learning, with prover cost achievable on resource-constrained client devices and aggregate verifier cost on the server sublinear or efficient in the number of clients.

2. Client-directed verification of multi-party-dependent statements. Construct a (possibly interactive) ZKP or NIZK that allows the server (or another designated prover) to convince an individual client that a statement S depending on the joint inputs of many clients holds — for instance, that the published global model was correctly aggregated from valid client updates, that a claimed differential-privacy noise was added correctly, or that a particular client's contribution was included — without revealing the other clients' inputs and while producing a statement that the verifying client can meaningfully trust given that it has no direct access to the other clients' data.

The problem is to determine whether such protocols can be instantiated with end-to-end efficiency (prover time, verifier time, proof size, setup) suitable for deployment in federated learning at realistic scales, and to provide concrete constructions together with security proofs, or alternatively to establish lower bounds ruling out such efficient constructions.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent works (2023–2025), including zkFL, ProxyZKP, VPFL, and various verifiable-FL surveys, give NIZK/zk-SNARK constructions for proving properties of client updates and for verifying aggregation, with reported speedups over generic zk-SNARKs and Bulletproofs. However, no construction is known that simultaneously delivers practical prover cost on resource-constrained clients, sublinear server verification at federated scale, and full coverage of multi-party-dependent client-side verification statements; the general question of efficient ZKP/NIZK for federated learning remains an active open research direction.

status_evidence.title: zkFL: Zero-Knowledge Proof-based Gradient Aggregation for Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: Clients generate verifiable proofs for local updates and submit concise proofs to the server for efficient verification.
status_evidence.claim: Partial progress: NIZK-based gradient aggregation protocols have been proposed for FL.

status_evidence.title: SoK: Verifiable Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: Systematization of knowledge on verifiable federated learning surveying ZKP-based approaches and remaining challenges.
status_evidence.claim: The problem remains an active research area with multiple competing partial solutions.

status_evidence.title: A polynomial proxy model approach to verifiable decentralized federated learning
status_evidence.snippet: ProxyZKP achieves proof generation times 30–50% faster than zk-SNARKs and Bulletproofs.
status_evidence.claim: Efficiency improvements exist but full practicality across all FL settings is not yet achieved.

status_evidence.title: Zero-Knowledge Federated Learning: A New Trustworthy and Privacy-Preserving Distributed Learning Paradigm
status_evidence.snippet: Proposes a ZK-FL paradigm integrating zero-knowledge proofs into FL training and verification.
status_evidence.claim: Ongoing work on integrating ZKPs into FL, indicating the question is partially addressed.
